deck.topic: New build inspections: the pre drywall window and the eleven month warranty visit
deck.hook: Drywall goes up Thursday. What it hides is permanent.

points.title: The Pre Drywall Window
body: Before the walls close, every wire, pipe, duct and brace is sitting there in the open.
The day sheetrock goes up, all of it is sealed in for the life of the house.
You will not see it again until something leaks or trips.
points.loop: You are told it already passed.

points.title: That Stamp Is Not For You
body: The city inspector is checking code minimum on behalf of the city.
He is on site for minutes and he is not looking out for your future repair bill.
Passing and built well are two different results.

points.title: Two Visits, Not One
body: Hire your own independent inspector at frame stage, then again before closing.
It runs a few hundred per visit and it is the cheapest money you will spend on the house.
The builder cannot keep you out. They will just act like nobody asks.
points.loop: Then comes the day everyone rushes.

points.title: Blue Tape Is Not A List
body: At the final walkthrough they hand you tape and you mark scuffs and nail pops.
Tape on a wall is not a promise. It falls off and it proves nothing.
Get every item written, numbered and signed with a date next to it.

points.title: Month Eleven
body: Most builder warranties on the small stuff run twelve months from closing.
A full season of heat, cold and settling shows you what the house actually does.
Bring your inspector back one more time while it is still their problem.
points.loop: Most people miss it by weeks.

cta.payoff: the new build inspection checklist I hand my buyers. Exactly what to look at before drywall, what to write down at the final walkthrough, and the items to chase before your warranty year quietly ends.

linkedinCaption:
New construction has two inspection windows most buyers never use.

The first is at frame stage, before drywall. Every wire, pipe, duct and brace is visible. Once sheetrock goes up, none of it is seen again until something fails. The city inspector who signs off is checking code minimum on behalf of the city, not protecting your future repair bill.

The second is month eleven. Most builder warranties on smaller items expire at twelve months from closing. One full season of heat, cold and settling reveals what the house actually does.

Blue tape at the walkthrough is not documentation. Written, numbered, dated and signed is documentation.

For those of you building or representing buyers on new construction, how are you handling the eleven month visit?
